title: Game 6: Hans vs Magnus
notes: Game 6 of 12 in the experiment, from the Sicilian Defence, Najdorf. Magnus (the learner) reads his notebook and similar past mistakes before every move; Hans (the control) has neither.

This is the Najdorf Sicilian, and I want a solid developing move that prepares f3, Qd2 and a kingside pawn storm — Be3 (the English Attack) fits perfectly. Black's main replies like e5 or Ng4 are handled by Nb3 or Bg5/Bc1, and nothing is hanging since Be3 is defended by the queen after development.

I checked 6...Nxe4 first: 7.Nxe4 d5 8.Bd3 just leaves me a pawn down with no support for the knight, so the pawn is poisoned. Instead the main-line English Attack reply 6...e5 gains central space, hits the d4 knight with tempo, and if 7.Nf5 I answer ...d5 or ...Bxf5 — I keep development flowing without loose pieces.

Black's 6...e5 hits my d4-knight, and in this English Attack structure the main retreat is Nb3, keeping the knight active, eyeing a5/c5 and supporting a future f3/Qd2 with queenside expansion. Alternatives like Nf3 block my f-pawn and Nf5 lets Black gain time with ...d5 or trade favorably after ...Bxf5.

Nxe4 fails to 8.Nxe4 d5 9.Bb5+ winning a pawn, so I avoid the greedy capture as my rules demand. Instead I play the main-line 7...Be6, developing, covering d5 against Nd5/Nc5 ideas and preparing ...Be7 and ...0-0 with no loose pieces left hanging.

This is the standard Najdorf structure after 6.Be3 e5 7.Nb3 Be6, where the main line is f3, securing e4 and preparing Qd2, g4 with a kingside pawn storm plus Nd5 ideas. Qxd6 is a blunder since d6 is doubly defended, and Bxa6 just loses a piece to Nxa6.

White's 8.f3 locks in his f1-bishop and weakens the e1-h4 diagonal, so the principled reply is the central break 8...d5 before White consolidates with Qd2/0-0-0. After 9.exd5 Nxd5 10.Nxd5 Bxd5 (or Qxd5) the trades leave material level with my strong e5 pawn, and I've checked that White has no checks or tactics against my loose pieces in that sequence.

review.label: inaccuracy
review.refutation: 9. exd5 Nxd5 10. Nxd5 Bxd5 11. Qd2 Be6

moves.thought: Black's 8...d5 is the standard counter, and the cleanest reply is to resolve the center with 9.exd5, after which Nxd5 10.Nxd5 Bxd5 11.Qd2/c4 leaves me with the bishop pair and pressure on the loose d5 bishop and the e5 pawn. Passive alternatives like Qd2 or Bf2 allow 9...d4 or ...dxe4 freeing Black's game, so I take at once.

I must recapture the d5 wedge at once (rule 11), and counting captures on d5 (rule 2): after 9...Nxd5 10.Nxd5 Bxd5 my bishop is defended by the queen, so 11.Qxd5 Qxd5 would lose White's queen for a bishop, leaving me with a strong centralised bishop and the e5 pawn. I also checked White's checks — Bb5+ simply drops to axb5 — so this book recapture is safe, whereas 9...Bxd5 10.Nxd5 Nxd5 surrenders my light-squared bishop and lets c4 harass the knight.

I must not play Bc4 (…Nxe3 wins a piece since Bxe6 Nxd1 nets Black the queen) and Qxd5 just drops the queen to …Bxd5, so I resolve the central tension favourably by trading on d5. After 10.Nxd5 Bxd5 I plan 11.c4 kicking the bishop, then Qxd8+ and Nc5/Bc5 pressure against b7 and the dark squares with Black's king stuck in the centre.

Recapturing with the bishop leaves it on d5 with no pawn able to support it, and c4 would chase it while White develops with Qd2/0-0-0 (that's exactly the position my library shows as comfortable for White); recapturing with the queen keeps my bishop usefully on e6, so 11.Bc4 simply loses a piece to Bxc4 and 11.Qxd5 Bxd5 trades off White's initiative.

review.label: inaccuracy
review.refutation: 11. Qxd5 Bxd5 12. O-O-O Be6 13. Na5 b5

moves.thought: Bc4 and c4-ideas looked tempting but c4 is only defended by Bf1, so 11.Bc4?? Qxc4 just drops a bishop. Trading queens with 11.Qxd5 Bxd5 suits me: I keep the bishop pair, and 12.c4 immediately kicks the centralized bishop while Black's knight is still stuck on b8.

White's queen on d5 is completely undefended (Nb3 covers c5/a5/d4, not d5), so I simply recapture with the bishop to restore material equality — anything else loses a queen for nothing. After Bxd5 I only need to watch c2-c4 chasing the bishop, which I can meet with Be6 or Bc6 while my structure stays sound.

Black's bishop on d5 is his best-placed piece, so I want to trade it off with Bc4; after Bxc4 Nxc4 my knight lands on an excellent square and immediately hits the loose e5 pawn, gaining a tempo while Black is still undeveloped. The alternative O-O-O leaves that bishop dominating the light squares.

My d5 bishop is attacked and unsupported (rule 8), and both Be4 and Bxf3 simply lose to pawn recaptures (fxe4 / gxf3), so I trade it off; after 12...Bxc4 13.Nxc4 the knight hits e5, but 13...Nc6 defends the pawn and develops, leaving a balanced, simplified queenless position.

My bishop on c4 was just taken and oddly I can't recapture, so I need to regain material by attacking the intruding bishop; Nd2 hits it immediately (and also covers e4/f3) while keeping my structure solid. Na5 also hits c4 and b7, but Black answers Bd5 defending both and my knight ends up stranded on the rim, whereas after Nd2 Be6 I can follow with c3/b3 and castle to keep pressure.

I'm up a full bishop and Nd2 attacks my bishop on c4, so I just need a safe retreat: Bxa2 loses to Rxa2, Bd3 loses to cxd3, Bc5 drops the piece to Bxc5, and Bd5 invites c4 chasing it anyway. Be6 is attacked by nothing, keeps the extra piece, and lets me finish development with ...Nc6/...Be7 while White has no queen and no checks available.

With queens off, I want to develop and pressure Black's weak e5 pawn while Black's queenside knight is still on b8; Nc4 hits e5 with tempo. If Black plays b5 then Nxe5 nets a pawn, and Bxc4 or Nd7 just helps me centralize, so I'm comfortable with Nc4 before castling long next.

The knight just moved to c4 where my e6 bishop already attacks it, and I counted every possible defender — b2 and c2 pawns don't cover c4, Be3 isn't on that diagonal, and neither rook reaches it — so the knight is completely undefended. After Bxc4 White has no recapture and no intervening check or threat (Bc5 is met by the king guarding f8), so I simply win a clean piece.

I'm a knight down after the Nc4 blunder, so I need to fight for activity and gain tempi. b3 immediately attacks the strong bishop on c4 and forces it to retreat (Bd3 loses to cxd3), after which I can castle long and pressure the queenside and the e5 pawn.

My light-squared bishop on c4 is attacked by the b3 pawn, and Bxb3 would just lose it to cxb3, so I must retreat it; being a bishop and knight ahead I only need a safe square. Bd3/Be2/Bf1 all drop the bishop (cxd3, Kxe2, Kxf1/Rxf1), and Bd5 invites c2-c4 to chase it, so Be6 is the clean square that no pawn or piece can ever hit, keeping my huge material lead intact.

I'm down two pieces, so my priority is king safety and getting both rooks active to create practical chances; Black's bishop on e6 hits b3 but it's doubly defended. Castling short tucks the king away and brings the h1-rook to f1, keeping Bc5/Ba7 ideas and the f-file in reserve.

I'm up a bishop and a knight for nothing, so I just need safe development and simplification — Bxb3 would be a foolish piece-for-pawn since cxb3 recaptures. Nc6 develops my last piece with no enemy capture available on c6, prepares ...Be7 and castling, and leaves nothing loose for White's bishop or rooks to hit.

Material and structure are balanced with queens off, so I want to grab the only open file and keep pressure on Black's awkward king on e8. Rad1 takes the d-file while leaving my f1-rook to support a later f4 push against e5; Black's main try Rd8 just leads to an equal rook trade, and Bd6 blocks his own bishop.

I'm up a bishop and a knight, so I only need safe consolidation: Bxb3 fails to cxb3, Bd6 drops to Rxd6 on the open d-file, Bc5 drops to Bxc5, and Nd4 invites Bxd4 exd4 Rxd4 giving material back. Be7 is attacked by nothing, keeps every piece guarded, and prepares ...O-O to finish development before White gets any play on the d- and e-files.

I'm down two pieces from earlier blunders, so my only hope is maximum activity and pressure on the open d-file against Black's uncastled king. Rd2 prepares Rfd1 to double, keeping the d-file firmly under control without walking into Bxd5/Kxd7/Bxd6 tricks that the other rook advances allow.

I'm up a bishop and a knight, so I just need safety and simplification — Bxb3 would break my capture-count rule since cxb3 wins the bishop for a pawn. Castling tucks my king away, connects the rooks and leaves nothing loose for White's rooks or bishop to hit.

The position is a symmetrical rook-and-bishop endgame where Black's only slight weakness is the e5 pawn, so I want to pile up on it rather than lunge with Rd5 (which gets hit by Nd4). Re1 brings my idle rook to the half-open e-file while the other rook keeps the open d-file, and I checked that 19...Nd4 20.Bxd4 exd4 21.Rxd4 just trades off evenly.

I'm up a bishop and a knight, so my only job is to keep everything defended and simplify; scanning loose units I see my e5 pawn is undefended and White's Rd2-d5 (or a later rook trade followed by Rxe5) would snatch it. Bf6 guards e5, activates the bishop on the long diagonal, and leaves nothing capturable — unlike Nd4, which after Bxd4 exd4 Rxd4 hands back a free pawn.

I'm down material, so I want to keep pieces on and stay active rather than simplify; note that Rd7 and Rd5 are impossible since Black's bishop on e6 guards both squares. Bc5 develops the bishop to an active diagonal with tempo on the f8 rook, avoids the trade Black wants with Bf6, and keeps options like Bd6 pressuring e5.

White's Bc5 attacks my f8 rook, which is only defended by the king, so I must move it; being two pieces up I prefer the move that offers a trade of rooks. Rfd8 saves the rook and invites Rxd8+ Rxd8, simplifying toward an easily won ending, and nothing of mine hangs afterwards (e5 is still covered by Bf6, so Rxe5 just loses a rook).

I'm down two pieces after the earlier disaster on c4, and crucially my rook on d2 is hanging to Rxd8-no, to Rxd2 — Black's Rd8 attacks it and nothing defends it. So I must resolve the d-file: Rdd1 keeps the rook defended by Re1, maintains control of the open file, and avoids forcing the rook trade that would only speed up Black's win.

I'm up two minor pieces (White's bishop sacrifices on c4 were never recaptured), so the clearest path is mass simplification. Trading on d1 is completely safe — after 22.Rxd1 nothing of mine hangs (Be6 covers d7), and I can follow with ...Rd8 to trade the last rooks and convert with B+B+N against a lone bishop.

Black's rook has invaded on d1 and my rook on e1 is attacked, so recapturing is essentially forced — anything else like Bd4 loses the rook to Rxe1+. Since I'm already down material, I must avoid further losses and keep the position as simplified as possible.

I'm up two pieces (knight and bishop) for nothing, so the cleanest path is simplification: 22...Rd8 forces 23.Rxd8+ Bxd8, leaving me two bishops and a knight against a lone bishop. I checked Bxb3 (cxb3 or axb3 just wins my bishop, breaking rule 2) and Nd4 (Bxd4 exd4 Rxd4 gives material back), so the rook trade is best.

I'm down two pieces, so trades only help Black; I want to keep my rook active and my bishop annoying. Bd6 avoids the rook swap on d8 (Rxd6 would actually win material back for me), hits e5, and keeps the bishop on a strong square, whereas Rxd8+ just simplifies into a hopeless ending.

I'm up two pieces, so I want forcing simplification: 23...Be7 attacks the d6 bishop, and because the bishop is the only thing shielding White's undefended rook on d1, any bishop move (including Bxe5) runs into ...Rxd1+ winning a full rook. That leaves White only Bxe7 Nxe7 or Rxd8, both trading into a trivially won ending where I keep two extra pieces.

The key problem is that my rook on d1 is only shielded by the bishop on d6, so if that bishop moves or captures, Black wins the rook outright with ...Rxd1+ (nothing can recapture) — e.g. 24.Bxe7 Rxd1+ 25.Kf2 Nxe7 costs me a full rook plus the bishop. Moves like Rd3 or Rd5 don't help either, since after ...Bxd6 the recapturing rook on d6 just gets taken by Rd8. So I'll cut my losses: get the rook off the d-file to a safe, active square where it eyes e5, conceding only the bishop.

White's bishop on d6 is completely undefended, so I just take it free — I counted every white unit that touches d6 (none) and there are no checks or counter-captures available to White afterwards. I capture with the bishop rather than the rook so my rook stays active on the open d-file, leaving me up two pieces heading into a trivially won ending.

I'm hopelessly down material (a rook versus rook plus three pieces), so Rxe5 fails immediately to Nxe5 or Bxe5, and Rd1 just invites a rook trade that ends all resistance. I'll keep the rook on the board and bring my king toward the center with Kf2 to hold the dark squares and slow Black's pawn advance.

I'm up three pieces for nothing, so I only need safety: Bxb3 is a trap since cxb3 recaptures (rule 2), so I avoid it. Nd4 centralizes the knight on an untouchable square, eyes c2, b3, e2 and f3, and leaves nothing of mine loose; if White offers Rd1 I'll happily trade rooks into a trivially won ending.

I'm down a lot of material, so I need to stay solid and avoid further losses: Rxe5 fails to Bxe5 since the bishop on d6 guards that pawn, and Rd1 would just drop the rook to Rxd1 with no recapture. The knight on d4 is eyeing c2, so c3 kicks it with tempo (Nxb3 just loses the knight to axb3) and I can follow up with Rc1 or b4/a4 to gain some space.

The c3 pawn attacks my knight, and Nxb3/Bxb3 just lose a piece to axb3 while Ne2 drops the knight to Rxe2. Retreating with Nc6 puts the knight on a square defended by my b7 pawn, keeps e5 guarded by the bishop, and preserves my huge material edge (two bishops and a knight for nothing).

I'm down a lot of material, so I need to stay solid — Rxe5 just drops the rook to Bxe5 since the pawn is defended by the bishop on d6. Re4 gets kicked by Bd5 or f5, so I'll put the rook on e2 where it guards the second rank and supports f3/g2 while keeping the e-file.

I'm up two minor pieces, so I only need safety: Nd4 loses to cxd4 and Bc4 loses to bxc4, and Bxb3 drops a bishop to axb3 — all fail the "count the capturers" test. Rd7 is the solid consolidating move: it keeps b7 and the seventh rank guarded, leaves e5 doubly defended by Nc6 and Bd6, and prepares to invade on d2 or trade rooks into a trivially won ending.

I'm down three pieces for nothing, so my only job is to avoid further losses and keep my rook active — Rxe5 just drops the rook since both the bishop on d6 and knight on c6 guard that pawn, and Rd2 invites a rook trade that leaves a hopeless pawn ending. I'll play g3 to give my king shelter and squares while keeping the rook flexible on the second rank.

I'm up two pieces (B+B+N for nothing), so I just need a safe, active move with no tactics against me. Nd4 hits the rook on e2 and the f3/b3 pawns, and the knight is solidly supported by my e5 pawn, while 29.Rd2?? would simply drop the rook to Rxd2.

Black's knight just hopped back to d4 where it's attacked by my c3 pawn and defended only by the e5 pawn, so cxd4 exd4 nets me a full knight for a pawn. I'm still material down overall, so grabbing this piece is essential; Rxe5 would instead just lose my rook to Bxe5.

I'm up two bishops for nothing, so the simplest path is to grab the free pawn with exd4 — if White answers Rxe6 I recapture with fxe6 and win the rook for a bishop, leaving a trivially won R+B ending. If instead White plays Rd2 or Re4 I hold d4 with Bc5, and my e6 bishop is already guarded by the f7 pawn, so nothing of mine hangs.

I'm down two bishops for a rook here, so I need maximum activity: Re4 immediately attacks the loose d4 pawn and keeps my rook on an active file/rank. If Black hits my rook with Bf5 or Bd5 I simply retreat to e2, and I avoid Rxe6, which would just lose a rook for a bishop outright.

White's Re4 is hitting my d4 pawn, so I need a defence that isn't itself capturable — Be5 and Bd5/Bf5 all attack the rook but sit on undefended squares where Rxe5/Rxd5/Rxf5 just grabs a bishop. Bc5 defends d4 (Rxd4 Bxd4+) and no white unit can touch c5, keeping my two-bishop-plus-pawn advantage intact while I prepare ...d3 and a rook trade into a trivially won ending.

I'm material down, so I need activity rather than passivity; Re5 attacks the undefended bishop on c5 while also eyeing e6 and keeping the rook on the e-file to meet ...d3 with Re3. Capturing on d4 or e6 loses to ...Bxd4+ or ...fxe6, so the fork attempt is my best practical try.

My c5 bishop is attacked by the rook on e5, and I'm up two bishops, so I want a move that both saves it and gains time: 31...Bd6 hits the rook (it's defended by my Rd7 and no White unit can reach d6), forcing the rook to run while I keep all my extra material. I rejected Bxb3 since a2 simply recaptures, and preferred keeping rook plus two bishops over trading into bishops-versus-pawns.

My rook on e5 is attacked by the bishop on d6, and Rxe6 fxe6 would just dump the rook for a bishop while I'm already down material. Re4 steps away while attacking the loose d4 pawn, and it invites the same Bc5/Bd6 shuffle we've just had, giving me repetition chances in a bad position.

I'm up two bishops for one pawn, so simplification is the clearest path: 32...Re7 offers the rook trade (33.Rxe7 Bxe7 leaves two bishops plus five pawns against five pawns, a trivial win), and even if White declines with 33.Rxd4 Rxe... he only grabs a pawn while I keep both bishops. I avoided Bxg3+ (just loses a bishop to hxg3) and the loosening pawn pushes my mistake library punished.

I'm down two bishops, so I need to grab material and activity: the d4 pawn is actually undefended (the bishop on d6 and the rook on e7 don't cover it), so Rxd4 wins a free pawn. After Rxd4 Bc5 I answer Rd5 hitting the bishop, and if Black tries Rd7 I simply avoid the rook trade by sliding along the fourth rank, since trading rooks into a two-bishop endgame would be fatal.

I'm up two bishops with equal pawns, so I just need to keep everything safe and simplify; Bd5 and Rd7 both lose material to Rxd5 and Rxd6, while Bxb3/Bxg3+ simply drop a bishop to axb3/hxg3. Bc5 hits the undefended rook with tempo, keeps both bishops guarded from capture (nothing attacks c5), and if the rook tries Rc4 or Rd5 then Bxc4/Bxd5 wins it outright.

My rook on d4 is pinned along the c5–d4–e3–f2 diagonal, so it can't move, and b4 doesn't help since Bxd4+ still wins it outright. Ke3 is the only move that defends the rook: if 34...Bxd4+ 35.Kxd4 I at least get a bishop for it instead of losing the rook for nothing.

White's rook on d4 is attacked by my bishop and only the king defends it, so Bxd4+ trades a bishop for the rook and strips White of his last piece, leaving me rook plus bishop plus five pawns against a bare king and pawns. I checked that Kxd4 is White's only real reply and there are no forks or counter-threats left on the board, so this simplification is completely winning.

Black's bishop just captured on d4 with check, and nothing defends it — the rook on e7 and all the black pawns are out of range. Taking is forced in practice and wins back a piece, leaving me only a rook down instead of rook plus bishop.

Bxb3 would just lose the bishop to axb3, so I avoid that trap; instead I take the active option with Rd7+, driving White's king away from the centre and preparing Rd3 to fork the b3 and f3 pawns while my king walks in. With a whole rook and bishop extra against bare pawns, forcing simplification and pawn grabs is the cleanest win.

I must answer the rook check, and with my king I want to stay close to my remaining pawns while avoiding further harassment — Ke5 and Ke4 run into checks like Bd5+ or Rd5+ driving me back, and Kc5 strays from my kingside pawns. Ke3 is safe (neither Rd3+ nor Re7+ gains anything since d3 is undefended by the bishop) and keeps my king guarding the f3/g3/h2 cluster.

Bxb3 would just drop the bishop to axb3 (rule 2), and Rd2/Rd3+/Rd4 all lose the rook to the king on e3. So I play the quiet but active Rc7, planning Rc2 next to fork the a2 and h2 pawns while keeping my bishop flexible and out of any trap.

I'm down a rook and bishop for nothing, so my only practical chance is to keep the king as active as possible and try to create a blockade. Kd4 centralizes and eyes the queenside; Ke4 just invites ...Bd5+ with tempo, and retreating with Kd2/Kf2 leaves my pawns passive targets.

I'm a whole rook and bishop up, so my only job is to keep everything safe and grab pawns actively — Rc3, Rc4-ish squares and Rc5 are all touched by the d4 king, and Bxb3 just feeds the bishop to axb3. Rc2 is out of the king's reach, attacks both a2 and h2, and after Kd3 I simply take a free pawn with Rxh2 (or Rxa2) with the rook still safe.

I'm hopelessly down material (rook and bishop for nothing), so I just want the most active try: Kd3 attacks the rook on c2 and forces it to move, keeping my king central and gaining a tempo. Black will likely grab a pawn with Rxh2 or Rxa2, but there's nothing better available.

I'm a rook and bishop up against a bare king, so I just need safe, active material grabs: a2 is undefended (White's king on d3 doesn't reach it and there are no pieces left), and after Rxa2 the b3 pawn also falls to my bishop or rook. I checked that nothing of mine is attacked and White has no checks or captures at all.

I'm down a rook and bishop with no counterplay, so I just want to keep my remaining pawns alive as long as possible. My b3 pawn is hanging to the rook on a2, so Kc3 defends it while keeping the king active and centralized.

I'm up a whole rook and bishop, so I just need safe material grabs — Bxb3 is impossible since Kc3 guards b3, but h2 is completely undefended with White's king miles away on c3. Rxh2 wins a free pawn, keeps my rook active, and leaves White with no counterplay whatsoever.

I'm down a rook and bishop for two pawns, so I need activity and a queenside passer to create any practical chances. b4 advances my only real asset while staying protected by the king on c3, whereas Kd4 would drop the b3-pawn to ...Rb2.

I'm a whole rook and bishop up with no White pieces left, so I take the most active path: Rh3 hits both g3 and f3 along the third rank (g3 is undefended since f2 is empty, and no pawn can ever capture on h3), winning a pawn and keeping my own pawns connected and untouched.

I'm hopelessly down material (rook and bishop for two pawns), and my f3/g3 pawns can't both be saved from the rook on h3. Playing f4 connects the pawns so that after Rxg3 my f-pawn can push forward with gain of tempo on the bishop, and my king stays centralized.

I'm up a rook and bishop for nothing, and Rxg3+ simply snatches White's g-pawn with check — no White piece can recapture, and after the king steps away my bishop on e6 still covers f5 so the f-pawn can't run. That leaves White with a lone king and the b4 pawn against rook, bishop and five pawns.

I'm material down, so my only practical hope is an active king; Kd4 centralizes and heads toward e5/f6 where it supports the f-pawn and pressures Black's kingside. After Rg4+ Ke5 the f4 pawn is defended and my king gets active, whereas retreating with Kc2 or Kb2 just loses both pawns passively.

I'm up a rook and bishop for two pawns, so I just need safety and activity: Rd3+ loses the rook instantly to Kxd3, and Rf3 or Rb3 let the king approach with Ke4/Kc4 hitting my rook. Rg4 is on a square no White unit can reach while attacking the loose f4 pawn and keeping my rook active.

My f4 pawn is attacked by the rook on g4, so I want to defend it actively; Ke5 both guards f4 and attacks the bishop on e6. After Rg5+ I can step back to e4 and keep fighting, whereas passive king moves just lose the pawn immediately.

Rxf4 and Rg5+ both lose the rook (Kxf4 and fxg5), and the white king on e5 is annoyingly active hitting my bishop, so I want a forcing move that drives it back. f6+ is check (the pawn is covered by g7, so Kxf6 loses to gxf6) and forces the king to the d-file, after which Rxf4 picks up the last kingside pawn safely and my rook, bishop and four extra pawns win trivially.

The check with f6+ left the bishop on e6 completely undefended — no black pawn or piece covers that square anymore. Since I'm down a rook, grabbing the free bishop with Kxe6 is clearly the best practical try, keeping my b-pawn and active king.

White's king on e6 attacks f6 (defended by g7) but does not touch f4, so Rxf4 simply snaps off a free pawn with no recapture available. That leaves me a rook and five pawns against a lone b-pawn, which my rook easily stops from behind or in front; if Kf5 chases the rook, it just slides along the fourth rank and takes b4 too.

I'm down a full rook, so my only practical hope is counterplay with the b-pawn and my king raiding the queenside pawns. Kd7 heads for c7/b6 to pressure b7 and a6, while b5 just loses the pawn to axb5 immediately.

I'm up a rook for one pawn, so the simplest path is to grab White's last pawn with Rxb4, leaving king and rook plus four pawns against a bare king. The rook on b4 also guards b7 along the file, so Kc6/Kc7 wins nothing, and no check or capture is available to White.

I'm down to a bare king against rook and four pawns, so my only practical hope is grabbing material and running for a stalemate-ish resource. Kc7 attacks the loose b7 pawn and keeps my king active, whereas retreating moves just let Black advance unhindered.

White has only a bare king while I have rook plus five pawns, so nothing can be hung: b7 is defended by my rook along the b-file and a6 is defended by b7, so Kb6 achieves nothing. Rather than loosen the a6/b7 chain with a5 or b5 (which would drop a6 after Kb6), I activate my king toward the centre and prepare to escort the kingside pawns.

I'm down to a bare king against rook and five pawns, so the game is lost; Kxb7 isn't available since the rook on b4 guards it. I'll keep my king as active as possible with Kd6, staying near the black pawns and avoiding getting shoved into the corner.

I'm a rook and four pawns up against a bare king, so my only real danger is a loose rook — Rb6+, Rd4+ and Rb5 all lose the rook to Kc7, Kc5 and Kc6 respectively, since nothing defends it. Rb1 keeps the rook on the b-file guarding b7 (and thus a6) while sitting far out of the king's reach, so I can then walk my king up and push the pawns.

I'm a bare king against a rook and five pawns, so the game is lost; my only aim is to stay as central as possible and avoid being driven to the edge quickly. Kc7 would attack b7 but it's defended by the rook on b1, and Kd7/Kc5 drift toward the rim, so Kd5 keeps the king in the centre and makes Black work the longest.

I'm a rook and four pawns up against a bare king, so I just need a safe, active move with no stalemate or counterplay risk. Rb5+ drives the king off the fifth rank, keeps my b7 pawn protected along the b-file, and lets me bring my king and pawns forward next.

I'm down to a bare king against rook and three pawns, so my only practical hope is to harass the queenside pawns and seek stalemate tricks. Kc4 attacks the rook on b5 (though it's defended by the a6 pawn) and keeps my king near b7/a6, whereas Kd6/Ke4 just drift while Black consolidates.

White's Kc4 attacks my rook on b5, and although a6 defends it, allowing Kxb5 axb5 would throw away the rook for nothing. I retreat to b1, far from the king and still cutting the b-file, so I keep rook plus four pawns against a bare king and can simply escort my pawns home.

I'm down to a bare king against a rook and three pawns, so my only practical chance is maximum king activity against Black's queenside pawns. Kc5 heads for b6/a6 and keeps my king out of immediate rook checks, whereas Kd3/Kc3 would just retreat passively.

I'm a rook and three pawns up against a bare king, so the cleanest plan is to cut the white king off and march the kingside pawns. Rb5+ is safe because the a6 pawn defends b5, the rook simultaneously guards b7, and after the king retreats it is confined to ranks 1-4 while my king and f/g/h pawns promote unopposed.

new_lessons: [middlegame] Before any quiet or developing move, scan every enemy check; if a check (Qh4+/Qa5+ when f3 is played or the king sits uncastled) wins your piece, choose differently Example: 11.Bc4?? Qh4+ 12.Bf2 Qxc4: f3 plus uncastled king made the e1-h4 check decisive, 55%→8%

[middlegame] Count every unit that can capture your destination square and play out the whole recapture sequence; move only if the final material count favours you Example: ...Qc3 forked rooks but bxc3 won the queen; 26.Ne5 Rxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 gave two knights for a rook

[endgame] Never place a piece on a square the enemy king attacks unless your own piece guards it; test Kx and stalemate first, even when winning easily Example: 66...Qc3+? Kxc3 drew a won Q endgame; later 58...Rd4 let 60.Kxd4 take my rook

[endgame] With overwhelming material, improve king and rook first (cut the enemy king off, seventh rank) and advance pawns only when king or rook escorts them Example: 59...b5 pushed an unescorted pawn instead of Rd5; loose pawns and a stray rook let the king counterattack

[endgame] When material ahead, welcome equal trades and simplify: rook plus pawns beats bishop plus pawns; only bare rook versus bishop is drawn Example: Refusing 31.Rd5 trade "to keep the exchange" dropped winning chances 94%→61%

[opening] Delay the central break (...d5/...e5) until your minor pieces are out and your king is castled; otherwise the opened lines favour the developed side Example: 8...d5 exd5 with Nb8 and king home left a backward e5 pawn and open e-file, 48%→42%

[opening] When two pieces can recapture, prefer the minor piece; recapturing with the queen onto a square the enemy queen eyes just hands them the trade for free Example: 10...Qxd5? 11.Qxd5 Bxd5 reached the same structure a tempo down with queens gone, 45%→38%

[middlegame] Each move name your undefended pieces and the entry squares (c2, d3, g4, your sixth/seventh rank) an enemy piece can reach; guard the loosest before acting Example: Loose bishop plus loose pawn gave Black free tempi ...Nb4, ...d5, ...f5; the rook then invaded d6-c6

[middlegame] Keep a knight or bishop on an advanced central square only if a pawn can support it; otherwise retreat before pawns chase it into having no squares Example: Unsupported Ne4 had no safe retreat after e5/d6; Bd5 and Be4 were chased by pawns

[middlegame] Never push pawns in front of your king while an enemy bishop or queen eyes those squares; answer a wing pawn storm with a central break or file-opening capture Example: 17.g3 invited fxg3 and Bxh3; 17.dxc6 kept a winning game

[endgame] Before your king or rook grabs material, count the pawn race and confirm your king stays inside the square of every enemy passer Example: 44...Kxh4 won a rook but f4-f5-f6 plus the h-pawn made two queens

[opening] When your bishop is attacked, pick the retreat that checks or gains a tempo and prevents the opponent's planned central push, not the passive square Example: 6...Bb6 instead of Bb4+ allowed e5 and the d6 wedge; chances fell 50%→32%

[opening] When an enemy pawn wedges into your camp on the sixth or seventh rank, capture or blockade it immediately; trades that leave it alive cost material Example: 10...Nxd2 ignored the d6 pawn; d6-d7xe7 then wrecked my structure
